name: Dana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day on the lines involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the district line crew along the wooded roads. We replace old fittings, clear branches and sometimes work into the night after a windstorm. I earned a two-year technical diploma, but I still listen for a loose fitting before I touch it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes the job harder now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The cold gets into my shoulders, and my husband Ray cannot return to his old driving job after hurting his back. My wage covers most of our bills. I never use AI tools; a checked work order and a call to dispatch suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can have its little shortcut if the pole numbers remain right. Wind still brings trees down on the district lines, and we still go out to clear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Ray cannot do his old driving work after his back injury, so my lineworker pay carries most of the house. We have about four months saved and some nearby line jobs, which is enough to keep me steady but not careless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the district repair crew and check the storm kit before winter. I would keep our planned monthly transfer into savings from my wage, with no reason to change the amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. The work is there, although Ray and I count the cost of heating every winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the heating cost change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have already set a household limit and put the heavier curtains back up. I would not call this an AI response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using the office AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The dispatcher can use it, and I will read the printed work order and check the site as I always do.

say: I would accept a small **office shortcut** if pole numbers remain correct.
I would tell the crew that **storm lines** still need people to clear trees and repair fittings.
think: My wage carries most bills since Ray’s **back injury** ended his driving work.
Our **four-month cushion** gives some room, though winter heating still needs watching.
do: Keep leading **district repairs** and check the storm kit before winter.
Continue the existing **monthly savings** transfer from wages at its current amount.
feel: **Calm** about work, with familiar concern about winter heating bills.
S0.quote: Wind still brings trees down on the district lines, and we still go out to clear them.
fieldNote: Her modest reserve and typical pay support **steady work**, while Ray no longer brings a driving wage.
She explicitly keeps an **existing savings rate**, so no new save-more action follows.

steps.text: Keep leading district line repairs and checking the storm kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the depot to put a real name on every AI work order. A plan can book a truck, but it cannot see a rotten pole from a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may get leaner and ask each crew to take more calls. I think my field hours will hold for now, but I worry the faster schedules could squeeze our overtime, which pays for Ray’s physical therapy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare three monthly rosters with the therapy invoices before we make any big purchase. If overtime falls, we would delay replacing the dining room flooring and use the existing savings for therapy only if necessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can work fast in a storm, but I cannot promise how the depot will pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a bad work order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its pole number with the map and call dispatch before the truck goes up the hill. If they cannot name a checker, I will write the problem on the job sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Ray take a cheaper therapy slot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He already takes the least expensive appointment we could find nearby. Cutting my husband Ray’s therapy visits without his therapist saying so would be a false saving.

say: I would demand a **named checker** on AI work orders before a storm truck leaves.
I would remind the depot that **rotten poles** must be checked on site.
think: My field hours may hold, but **overtime** could shrink under faster scheduling.
Ray’s **therapy bills** depend on that extra pay more than our household likes to admit.
do: Compare three **monthly rosters** with Ray’s therapy invoices.
Delay the **dining flooring** if overtime falls rather than cut therapy visits.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic fall in overtime supporting Ray’s treatment.
S1.quote: Cutting my husband Ray’s therapy visits without his therapist saying so would be a false saving.
fieldNote: She distinguishes likely continued field work from possible **overtime loss**.
The spending cut is **flooring**, conditional on a real pay reduction; she protects therapy visits.

steps.text: Delay dining room flooring if storm overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 can make a work order, but it cannot clear a fallen tree. If capable robots reach the line around 2031, I would insist on watching one work in a real storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three by the robot date and might still need the wage because Ray is not working. I think the depot could reduce our crew before then, especially if planning gets cheaper, and four months saved would go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the storm rota while there are shifts. If the depot cuts my hours for two months, I would apply to the nearby line contractors and ask Ray to go through our bills with me before we touch the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed when I think of the house running on one wage. There is a plan, though, and other line jobs exist within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which contractor would you contact first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one that maintains the eastern feeder; I have worked beside its crews on storm days. I would ask about actual paid hours before considering a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the company before a cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A known wage and four months saved are better than a guess about a contractor. I would move only for a firm offer with enough hours.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** writes orders, while 2031 robots would need testing on real storm repairs.
I would insist a **field crew** watches a capable robot before it touches a damaged line.
think: Ray cannot replace his old **driving wage**, and I may need line work beyond 2031.
A **crew reduction** could drain four months of savings before I find another post.
do: Keep the **storm rota** while company field shifts continue.
Apply to **nearby line contractors** after two months of cut hours, seeking a firm paid offer.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible hours cut, with a reserve and nearby alternatives giving some control.
S2.quote: I would move only for a firm offer with enough hours.
fieldNote: Her robot exposure arrives after the thinking date, but she expects **possible earlier crew pressure**.
The job search has a **two-month trigger** and any move depends on a firm offer with adequate hours.

steps.text: Keep taking company storm shifts while field hours continue
Apply to nearby line contractors after two months of cut hours for a firm paid offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to find out whether a repair robot survives wind and ice. I would let the maker demonstrate it, then ask the crew what failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 might change dispatch, but my climbing work continues until robots come around 2034. I would hope to have retired by then if Ray and I can afford it; I am not counting on a fixed payment or a magic date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the crew going next year and ask our household adviser to put the retirement figures on paper. I would also pay an extra small amount off the van loan from regular wages if therapy and heating bills leave room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the trade changing, but not expecting an immediate loss of my own pay. The extra years give us time to check what we can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would go to the van loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps thirty a month after the winter bills are known. I will not promise it while therapy costs are moving around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you bring retirement forward because of the 2034 robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our retirement income and bills should set my linework exit date, not repair robots arriving around 2034.

say: I would ask for **wind and ice trials** before 2034 repair robots replace field judgement.
I would listen to the **crew findings** after a maker’s demonstration.
think: My **climbing shifts** likely continue past the 2031 thinking date.
I hope to leave before **2034**, but only if household figures support it.
do: Keep **district repairs** going next year while field shifts remain.
Pay an extra **van loan amount** from wages only if therapy and heating leave room.
feel: **Uneasy** about a changing trade while my current wage still looks secure.
S3.quote: Our retirement income and bills should set my linework exit date, not repair robots arriving around 2034.
fieldNote: She wants a retirement calculation, yet makes **no early-exit commitment**.
The extra debt payment is **new saving** only if therapy and winter costs leave actual spare cash.

steps.text: Keep leading district repairs while company field shifts remain
Pay extra van loan principal from wages only if therapy and heating leave room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger workers there is time to learn storm faults before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still want a human name beside every cleared live-line job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our bills and health allow, I expect to have finished regular climbing before the thinking date. Ray’s therapy may still cost us, but the machines in this long picture are not likely to cut my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the storm crew this year and show the new apprentice how to spot a split crossarm after wind. Ray and I would review the household costs each spring before we settle when I stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own shifts, with a bit of sadness that the younger crew may work differently. At least they have years to learn the things the screen cannot smell or hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can a screen miss after wind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The burnt smell at a failing connection and a loose fitting tapping against the pole. I make the apprentice stand quietly for a minute before they reach for a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop earlier because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The date Ray and I choose will come from our accounts and health. I will not leave paid work just to beat a future machine.

say: I would make time for **storm-fault teaching** before thinking AI and later robots arrive.
I would still require a **named human** on live-line repair sign-off.
think: My current **field wage** looks safe through the years I expect to work.
Ray’s **therapy cost** still matters when we choose an affordable retirement date.
do: Keep the **storm crew** running and teach a new apprentice split-crossarm checks.
Review **household costs** with Ray each spring before settling a retirement date.
feel: **Calm** about my shifts, with some sadness for the changing trade.
S4.quote: I will not leave paid work just to beat a future machine.
fieldNote: She sees the long timeline as compatible with her **existing work plan**.
Retirement remains conditional on **household costs and health**, with no earlier exit triggered by the card.

steps.text: Keep leading storm repairs and teaching an apprentice split-crossarm checks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because crew hours could fall while Ray still needs therapy, well before robots can do storm repairs. A written staffing plan and firm paid offers from nearby contractors would help me decide what to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will take a call from a house without power at midnight. A repair robot cannot make the neighbour feel heard while the road is blocked.

headlineQuote: A repair robot cannot make the neighbour feel heard while the road is blocked.
portrait: **Dana**, 58, leads a district line crew with a technical diploma, typical pay and roughly four months of savings.
Her **husband Ray** no longer earns from driving, so overtime helps cover his therapy despite some nearby job alternatives.
She avoids **AI tools** and trusts site checks, while weighing retirement against household costs rather than a machine date.
The **2028 case** worries her because planning changes could cut crew hours before robots can clear storm lines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her crew hours while Ray still needs therapy.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan** and firm paid offers from nearby contractors would help her decide.
